blocks.text: Sales & Scoping Guide
Local Business Web Service — Internal Reference

This guide is for you — the person selling and scoping websites. It covers the retainer math, the ownership pitch, how to scope a project, and how to handle common prospect objections. Keep it close during sales conversations.
1. The Business Model (in one paragraph)

We build custom, hand-coded websites for local businesses using a reusable config-driven starter kit. Each client gets a fully custom site — different content, different design, different structure — built quickly from the same base. The site is theirs to own, hosted on a free-tier platform with no ongoing platform fees. Our revenue comes from a one-time build fee plus a monthly Care Plan retainer that handles hosting management, monitoring, support, and content edits. The retainer is the point — it's predictable recurring revenue, and it's what keeps the client's site healthy over time.
The pitch is simple: you own your site, we care for it, and you pay less over time than a builder subscription while actually owning something. That's the whole model. Everything else is details.

blocks.text: Why we lead with the retainer

items: The retainer is the predictable part. The build fee is one-time and varies by project. If you lead with the build fee, you're negotiating a one-time number. If you lead with the Care Plan, you're selling an ongoing relationship — which is what the client actually needs.
The retainer is what makes the business sustainable. A one-time build business is feast-or-famine. A retainer business has a baseline.
The retainer is what makes the site actually get cared for. Without an ongoing relationship, the site gets built, launched, and abandoned. That's not what we sell.

blocks.text: 3. The Ownership Pitch (memorize this)
This is the core pitch. Say it in your own words, but hit these points every time.
The builder problem

items: Most small business owners already tried a website builder. They're frustrated. They're paying $30–$100/month and still can't get the site to look or work the way they want.
They don't realize they don't actually own anything. If they stop paying, their site disappears. Their content is trapped in a platform. Their domain may be locked in.
They think they're renting a website. What they're actually renting is a cage — a proprietary system that holds their content hostage and charges them forever for access to their own business.

blocks.text: What ownership means

items: You own the site files. They live on a hosting provider, but they're yours — like files on your computer. You can move them, copy them, hand them to someone else.
You own your domain. It's registered in your name. You control where it points. No one can hold it hostage.
You own your content. Every word, every photo, every testimonial. It belongs to your business, not to a platform.
You have a human being who knows your business and answers the phone. Not a chatbot. Not a forum. A person.
The site is built from plain text files — not a proprietary visual builder. You're never trapped in a system you can't escape.

blocks.text: The comparison that lands

Own your site. $97/month builder subscriptions cost $3,492–$28,800 over three years and you own nothing. With us you own the site outright, get a hand-built design, local SEO, and a human who answers the phone.

Key insight: this pitch works because it's true. The numbers are real. The ownership is real. The frustration with builders is real and widely shared. You're not selling a feature — you're selling a better relationship with your own business's online presence.
4. Scoping a Project
Scope before you quote. A bad scope leads to a bad price, which leads to an unhappy client, which leads toScope creep, which leads to you working for less than you should. Don't do any of that.
The scoping conversation

items: Start with the business, not the website. Ask: what does this business do? Who are their customers? What do they want the website to do for them? What's currently working or not working?
Ask about their current online presence: Do they have a site now? What do they like/dislike about it? Do they have a Google Business Profile? Social media? Online reviews?
Ask about their goals: More foot traffic? More phone calls? Online bookings? A better first impression? Build trust with new customers?
Ask about content: Do they have photos? Logos? Testimonials? Do they know their hours, services, and pricing clearly? This tells you how much content work is involved.
Ask about timeline: When do they want to launch? Is there an event, season, or deadline driving it?
Ask about budget: Not 'what's your budget?' but 'have you invested in a website before? What did you pay?' This gives you a sense of their expectations without putting a number in their head first.

blocks.text: Watch for scope creep signals

items: 'Can we also add...' — anything beyond the tier's scope goes in the quote, not the existing build
'My cousin's friend said...' — other people's opinions are not scope. Politely anchor back to what we agreed.
'I'll know it when I see it' — this is the most expensive phrase in web design. Push for specific, concrete preferences before the build.
'Can you also handle...' — if it's a different service (SEO campaigns, email marketing, e-commerce, content writing), that's a separate engagement, not a build add-on.
Any request that sounds like 'just one more thing' during the build — confirm it's in scope or quote it before doing it.

blocks.text: 5. Handling Common Objections
These come up every time. Have a real answer ready — not a script, but a genuine response that addresses the concern.
'I can do it myself on a builder for cheap'

You can. And in six months you'll either be frustrated that it doesn't look the way you want, or you'll have spent 40 hours building it yourself when you could have been running your business. The $2,000 Standard build pays for itself in time saved and a better result. And you own it — no subscription, no platform, no one who can turn it off.
'The monthly fee seems high for just hosting'

The Care Plan is not 'just hosting' — hosting is free (Netlify free tier, which we use). The $60/month covers: someone watching your site 24/7 so you don't have to, security updates so you're not vulnerable, renewal reminders so you never lose your domain, and a human who answers when something needs attention. The hosting itself costs you nothing. The Care Plan is for the relationship and the peace of mind. You can cancel it anytime and keep your site.
'Can I just pay once and be done?'

You can — the build fee is one-time. But a website that isn't maintained doesn't stay healthy. Links break. Software needs updates. Domains expire. A site that's 'done' in 2024 is a liability in 2027 if nobody's watching it. The Care Plan is how we make sure your site stays an asset, not a neglected thing that's broken when you finally need it. That said — you don't have to be on a Care Plan. You can take the site and manage it yourself. We'll hand it over cleanly and give you everything you need to do that.
'I already have a site — can you just fix it?'

Sometimes yes, sometimes no. If the existing site is on a builder platform or was built by someone who's gone, we may not be able to work with it directly. We can usually either (a) build a new site on our kit using your existing content, or (b) audit the existing site and tell you what's wrong and what it would take to fix it. Ask to see the current site first — don't quote a fix without looking.
'I need it cheaper / I don't have the budget'

Two options: (1) Reduce scope — go from Standard to Starter, drop the gallery, drop testimonials, keep the essentials. (2) Delay — if now isn't the right time financially, that's fine. The site will be here when you're ready. What we won't do is build a cheap site that doesn't serve the business, or discount below our floor. A bad website is worse than no website — it sends the wrong message to customers.
'How long will it take?'

5–7 days from when we have all your content. The bottleneck is almost always content — the checklist exists so you know exactly what to gather. The more complete your materials, the faster we launch. If you have everything ready, we can often turn a Starter site around in 3–4 days.

7. Qualification Signals
Not every prospect is a good fit. Qualify before investing time.
Good fits

items: Local business with a physical location or defined service area
Owns or is willing to own their domain
Has (or is willing to get) a Google Business Profile
Has content to put on the site — or is willing to create it
Understands that a website is an investment, not an expense
Values ownership and a real relationship over the cheapest option
Has a budget that can accommodate a $1,000+ build and $60+/month ongoing
Is the decision-maker or can reach the decision-maker easily

blocks.text: Poor fits (decline or refer out)

items: Wants a $100 website — not our market; refer to a template or builder solution
Won't own their domain — walk away; this always ends badly
Expects a website to fix a broken business — the site amplifies what's already there, it doesn't fix fundamentals
Has no content and no intention of creating it — a site without content is an empty building
Isn't the decision-maker and can't get buy-in — you'll spend time and get nowhere
Wants ongoing work that's outside our model (e-commerce, complex web apps, ongoing content campaigns) — refer to the right specialist
Treats the website as a one-time purchase with no ongoing relationship — this is the opposite of what we sell; don't force it

blocks.text: 8. The Project Agreement (what it should cover)
A clear agreement prevents most problems. Make sure every project has one in writing before work starts.

items: Scope: Exactly what's being built, what tier, what's included. Reference the Content Checklist as the content that will be used.
Timeline: Estimated build duration and launch date, contingent on content being delivered on time.
Payment: Build fee amount, deposit (typically 50% to start, 50% on completion), when invoices are due.
Revisions: Number of revision rounds included (2), what counts as a revision (vs. a new feature or scope change), what happens after the included rounds.
Care Plan: The monthly retainer they're signing up for, what it covers, how to cancel (30 days' notice), what happens at cancellation.
Ownership: Clear statement that the client owns the site files, domain, content, and analytics data. We retain the starter kit framework IP.
Accounts: Statement that we set up third-party services (Formspree, Calendly, Netlify, Google Business Profile) in the client's accounts, not ours. List of accounts and access.
Content responsibility: The client is responsible for providing accurate, complete content by the agreed date. Delays in content delay launch.
What's not included: A clear list (copywriting, photography, logo design, advanced SEO, e-commerce, etc.) so there are no surprises.

Termination: Either party can end the agreement. If the client terminates during the build, the deposit is retained and any work completed is delivered. If we terminate (rare), we deliver what's done and refund the unearned portion.
Signatures: Both parties sign before work begins.

blocks.text: 10. Red Flags in a Sales Conversation

items: They won't talk about budget at all — either they have none, or they're not serious
They want everything for free or for a nominal fee — not a fit; refer out
They won't own their domain or want to discuss it — walk away; this always causes problems
They're more interested in arguing about the builder they already use than in understanding the alternative — they're not ready
They want a website to fix problems that are not website problems — a bad business with a good website is still a bad business
They want to skip the content checklist and 'just build it' — the build will be delayed and frustrating for both of you
They treat you like a commodity and compare you only to the cheapest builder — they're not valuing what you actually offer; this is a pricing trap
They're interested but won't make a decision or commit to a timeline — they may be shopping around; be helpful but don't chase indefinitely
They want a custom site but balk at the Standard tier price — the gap between what they want and what they'll pay is a problem; address it directly or decline

blocks.text: 11. Positioning Reminders

items: Never compete on price against builders. Compete on ownership, quality, and relationship. If you're the cheapest option, you've already lost.
The Care Plan is the product. The build is the on-ramp. Sell the relationship first, the site second.

The ownership pitch is your strongest differentiator. Builders can't offer it because their business model depends on renting access. You can offer it because your business model depends on keeping clients happy over time.
Don't overpromise. A small, well-built site that does what it's supposed to do is better than a bloated site with features nobody uses.
The Content Checklist exists for a reason — it prevents the most common cause of build delays. Send it early and be clear about its importance.
A happy client who refers another client is worth more than a marginally higher price from a reluctant one. Don't sacrifice the relationship for the sale.
If a prospect isn't a fit, say so. Referring them to something better for their situation builds trust and reputation. Chasing bad fits burns time and energy.

blocks.text: 13. Quick Retention Reference
Things that keep clients on the Care Plan and happy.

items: Monthly report (Care Plan+): A short email with uptime status, any changes made, and a glance at analytics. Even if nothing happened, send it. It shows you're paying attention.
Domain renewal reminders: Send these well before expiry (60 days, 30 days, 14 days, 7 days). Losing a domain is the worst outcome and entirely preventable.
Google Business Profile check-ins: Periodically check that hours, photos, and info are current. This directly affects local visibility.
Content edit responsiveness: Turnaround on Care Plan edits should be fast and predictable. This is the most visible part of the service day-to-day.
Check in after major holidays or seasons: 'Everything still looking right? Anything you want to update for the season?' — a small touch that shows you're thinking about their business.

Be proactive about problems: If something looks off, tell them before they notice. A client who hears about a problem from you before they see it themselves trusts you more than one who finds out on their own.
End-of-year check-in: A brief year-end note — what happened on the site this year, any recommendations for next year. Keeps the relationship warm and surfaces opportunities.
